summary: Defines the properties of the QUIC transport protocol that hold for all versions of the protocol. These invariants are the parts that networks and endpoints can rely on staying the same as QUIC evolves.

eli5.summary: QUIC will keep changing, but a few things never change. This lists those fixed things so everyone can count on them.

questions: which parts of quic stay the same across versions

subtitle: The short list of QUIC properties that every version must keep, so new versions can always be deployed.

tldr.problem: QUIC is meant to change over time through new versions, but endpoints and the networks between them need a few facts that never change, or no new version could be deployed safely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the invariants: QUIC packets ride in UDP datagrams, the first byte's high bit picks a long or short header, the long header carries a 32-bit version and connection IDs, and version 0 is reserved for version negotiation.
tldr.outcome: Anything not listed may change between versions. A protocol that does not follow these properties is not QUIC. The RFC is updated by RFC 9368.

facts.label: Connection ID length
facts.value: 0 to 255 bytes in a long header

facts.label: Header type bit
facts.value: High bit of first byte: 1 long, 0 short

sections.title: An Extremely Abstract Description of QUIC
sections.content:
QUIC is a connection-oriented protocol between two endpoints. Those endpoints exchange UDP datagrams, and the datagrams contain QUIC packets. Endpoints use QUIC packets to establish a QUIC connection, which is shared protocol state between them.

That is the whole starting picture. Everything else in this RFC is about which details of that picture a later version is not allowed to change.
sections.eli5: Two computers pass notes in envelopes (UDP datagrams). Inside each envelope are smaller notes (QUIC packets) that let them keep up a shared conversation.

sections.title: What Stays Fixed Across Versions
sections.content:
QUIC can negotiate a version, which lets the protocol change as requirements change. This RFC describes the subset that is intended to stay stable as new versions are developed and deployed. All of these invariants are independent of the IP version.

The primary goal is to make sure new versions of QUIC can be deployed. By documenting what cannot change, the RFC preserves the ability of endpoints to negotiate changes to everything else. A side effect is that it also fixes a minimal amount of information that is visible to anyone other than the endpoints.

Unless this document specifically prohibits a change, any aspect of the protocol can change between versions. The RFC also says it places requirements on future QUIC versions even where it uses no normative language.
sections.eli5: It is like agreeing that every edition of a board game keeps the same box shape. Inside the box, anything can change.

sections.title: Long and Short Headers
sections.content:
A UDP datagram holds one or more QUIC packets, but the invariants only describe the first packet in a datagram. There are two header types, told apart by the most significant bit of the first byte: set means a long header, cleared means a short header.

A long header has the form bit set to 1, 7 version-specific bits, a 32-bit Version, then a Destination Connection ID Length (8 bits) and Destination Connection ID, then a Source Connection ID Length (8 bits) and Source Connection ID. Each connection ID is between 0 and 255 bytes long. The rest of the packet is version-specific.

A short header has the form bit cleared to 0, 7 version-specific bits, and a Destination Connection ID that follows the first byte immediately. It has no version, no length fields and no source connection ID. The length of its destination connection ID is not encoded and is not constrained by the RFC.

Apart from these values, the payload is version-specific and of arbitrary length. QUIC packets might be integrity protected, including the header, but Version Negotiation packets are not.
sections.eli5: The first thing on every note tells you whether it is a long form with a full address block or a short form with just the recipient's name tag.

sections.title: Connection IDs and Versions
sections.content:
A connection ID is an opaque field of arbitrary length. Its main job is to make sure that changes in addressing at lower layers (UDP, IP and below) do not cause packets for a connection to go to the wrong QUIC endpoint. Endpoints and the intermediaries that support them use it to deliver each packet to the correct instance of an endpoint.

Each endpoint picks its connection IDs using version-specific methods, and packets for the same connection might use different connection ID values.

The Version field is a 4-byte identifier that endpoints can use to identify a QUIC version. The value 0x00000000 is reserved for version negotiation, and all other values are potentially valid. A protocol that does not conform to these properties is not QUIC.
sections.eli5: A connection ID is like a name tag on a lunch box. Even if the lunch box moves to a different table, the tag still tells people whose it is.

sections.title: Version Negotiation
sections.content:
An endpoint that receives a long header packet with a version it does not understand or support might send a Version Negotiation packet. Short header packets never trigger it. The packet is a long header packet whose Version field is 0x00000000.

After the connection ID fields it carries a list of Supported Version fields, each naming a version the sender supports, and no other fields. An endpoint MUST ignore a packet with no Supported Version fields or with a truncated one. The 7 bits after the form bit are Unused: they can be anything when sent and MUST be ignored on receipt.

The sender MUST echo the connection IDs back, swapped: the Destination Connection ID is taken from the received Source Connection ID, and the Source Connection ID from the received Destination Connection ID, which a client initially picks at random. This gives the client some assurance that the server received its packet and that an attacker who cannot see packets did not forge the reply.

The packet has no integrity or confidentiality protection. A receiving endpoint might change the version it uses afterwards, depending on the version it chooses. RFC 9000 describes how version 1 generates and consumes these packets.
sections.eli5: If you speak to someone in a language they do not know, they can hand back a card listing the languages they do speak. They copy your name tag onto it so you know it is an answer to you.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Middleboxes could watch the traits of one QUIC version and assume that other versions showing similar traits mean the same thing. Some effort went into removing or hiding observable traits in version 1, but many remain, and other versions may behave differently.

The version number is not in every packet, so a middlebox that wants to use version-specific traits reliably has to keep state for every connection ID it sees.

Because Version Negotiation packets are not integrity protected, they only have modest protection against insertion by attackers. An endpoint MUST authenticate the semantic content of a Version Negotiation packet if it tries a different QUIC version as a result.
sections.eli5: Do not assume you know what a note means just because it looks like an old one. And if a stranger hands you a card that says to switch languages, check that it is real first.

sections.title: Assumptions That Are Not Safe
sections.content:
Appendix A lists a sampling of traits of QUIC version 1 that anyone can observe but that are still free to change in a new version. Any of them can be false for a given version, and some are not even true for version 1. The list is illustrative, not exhaustive.

  • QUIC uses TLS, and some TLS messages are visible on the wire.
  • Long headers are only used while establishing a connection, and the first packets on a flow use a long header.
  • Packet numbers are encrypted, and they increase by one for every packet.
  • There is a minimum size for the client's first handshake packet, and the client speaks first.
  • The second bit of the first byte (0x40) is always set.
  • Only a server sends Version Negotiation, and receiving one makes an endpoint change version.
  • A connection ID changes infrequently.
  • The Version field is the same in both directions, and a given value means that version is in use.
  • Only one connection at a time exists between any pair of endpoints.
sections.eli5: Just because every edition so far had a certain feature does not mean the next one will. The list warns people not to count on habits that are not real rules.
